title: Bangladesh Measles Death Toll Climbs to 885 as Vaccination Gaps Fuel Ongoing Outbreak
excerpt: Nearly five months after the outbreak began, Bangladesh continues to lose an average of four children daily to measles, with over 130,000 suspected cases and public health experts warning the crisis remains far from controlled.
body:
• Bangladesh's measles death toll has reached 885, with five more children dying in the 24 hours reported on August 12, according to the Directorate General of Health Services.
  • Since the outbreak began in mid-March, over 131,000 suspected cases and more than 16,500 confirmed infections have been recorded, with approximately 800 new cases daily.
  • Public health experts blame critical gaps in vaccination coverage, with over 4 million children remaining unvaccinated despite a nationwide emergency campaign launched in April.
  • The outbreak disproportionately affects infants under six months who are too young for vaccination and children over five who were never vaccinated.

A Crisis That Won't Relent

Bangladesh's devastating measles outbreak has now claimed at least 885 lives, with the death toll continuing to rise despite months of emergency vaccination efforts. Five more children died with measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to August 12, according to data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).

https://x.com/anadoluagency/status/2087554711318929824

The outbreak, which began in mid-March 2026, has infected tens of thousands of children across the country. As of the latest DGHS data, there have been over 131,000 suspected cases and more than 16,500 laboratory-confirmed infections. Over 115,000 patients have been hospitalized since March 15, with approximately 111,000 having recovered.

Of the 885 deaths, the vast majority — nearly 790 — are classified as suspected measles deaths, while approximately 96 have been laboratory confirmed. The distinction reflects the challenges of testing capacity in a country where the healthcare system is severely strained by the outbreak's scale.

Why the Outbreak Persists

Public health experts have pointed to critical failures in Bangladesh's vaccination infrastructure as the root cause of the outbreak's persistence. Prof. Mahmudur Rahman, former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research and chair of the National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination, identified two vulnerable groups sustaining transmission.

"Nearly one-quarter of patients are infants under six months, who are too young to be vaccinated. At the same time, many children over five were never vaccinated. These two groups alone are enough to sustain transmission."

— Prof. Mahmudur Rahman, Chair, National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination

Rahman said the government's vaccination target underestimated the actual number of eligible children, leaving more than 4 million (40 lakh) children unvaccinated — far too many to achieve herd immunity.

The Vaccination Campaign's Shortcomings

Following the outbreak's acceleration in early April, the Bangladesh government launched a phased emergency measles vaccination campaign on April 5, targeting over 18 million (1.8 crore) children aged six months to under five years. While officials have claimed the campaign exceeded its targets, the continued daily toll tells a different story.

Hospitals across the country continue to report an influx of unvaccinated patients, exposing the gap between claimed coverage and actual protection on the ground. The DGHS has recorded an average of roughly 1,000 suspected and confirmed cases, 800 hospital admissions, and nearly four deaths per day throughout July and into August.

"The situation has improved, but not as much as expected two months after the vaccination campaign — the authorities do not appear to realise that," Rahman told The Daily Star.

A Broader Public Health Warning

The Bangladesh outbreak carries lessons that extend well beyond South Asia. Measles, one of the most contagious diseases known, requires vaccination coverage of approximately 95% to prevent outbreaks. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted routine childhood immunization programs worldwide, and multiple countries — including several in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa — have reported measles surges as a result.

For the South Asian diaspora community, the outbreak is a reminder of the importance of ensuring children's vaccination records are up to date, particularly before travel to the region. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that travelers to countries experiencing measles outbreaks ensure they have received two doses of the MMR vaccine.

What's Next

With the death toll showing no signs of plateauing, Bangladesh faces mounting pressure to expand its vaccination reach to the millions of children who remain unprotected. International health organizations, including the WHO, have been monitoring the situation, though large-scale international intervention has not yet materialized. The coming weeks will test whether the government's response can finally bend the curve on an epidemic that public health experts say should never have reached this scale.
